skills.name: Mass and weight; safety in the laboratory

note.text:
Mass is the amount of matter in a body; it is measured in kg with a balance and does not change from place to place.
Weight is the force of gravity on the body; it is measured in N with a newton meter and depends on the gravitational field strength g.
W = m × g. On Earth g ≈ 10 N/kg; on the Moon g ≈ 1.6 N/kg.
Safety: follow the teacher's instructions, wear goggles when needed, never taste chemicals, report breakages, keep the bench tidy, do not overload springs or balances.

sections.heading: Mass: how much matter
sections.text:
Mass measures how much matter is in a body. A {50} kg bag of cement has the same mass in Douala, on Mount Cameroon or on the Moon.
Its SI unit is the kilogram (kg), and it is measured with a balance (beam balance, electronic balance).

sections.heading: Weight: the pull of gravity
sections.text:
Weight is the force with which gravity pulls a body towards the Earth. Being a force, it is measured in newtons (N) with a newton meter.
Weight = mass × gravitational field strength: W = mg. On Earth g ≈ {10} N/kg, so a {5} kg mass weighs {50} N.
On the Moon g ≈ {1.6} N/kg, so the same mass weighs only {8} N. That is why astronauts can jump so high there.

sections.heading: Working safely
sections.text:
Physics practicals use glassware, heaters, springs and electricity.
• Follow the teacher's instructions and read the steps first.
• Wear goggles when heating or when something can splash.
• Never taste or directly smell chemicals.
• Report breakages and spills at once (mercury is poisonous).
• Do not overload springs and balances; keep the bench tidy.

key_words.meaning: the amount of matter in a body (kg)
the force of gravity on a body (N)
g, the weight of each kilogram ({10} N/kg on Earth)

examples: {2} kg of sugar weighs {20} N on Earth
{60} kg on the Moon weighs {96} N

mistake.right: "My mass is {55} kg; my weight is {550} N"
mistake.why: Kilograms measure mass. Weight is a force, measured in newtons.

worked_example.problem: Ngozi has a mass of {m} kg. Find her weight on Earth (g = {g} N/kg).

cards.idea: Weight = mass × g; on Earth g = {10} N/kg.
Mass stays the same everywhere; weight changes with g.
example: On the Moon the same {5} kg weighs only {8} N.

cards.idea: Safety first: follow instructions and report accidents at once.
example: Never taste or smell chemicals directly.

pick.q: A thermometer breaks and mercury spills on the bench. What should you do first?
pick.r: Tell the teacher at once and keep away from the mercury
w: Pick up the mercury with your fingers
Wipe it into the sink with water
Carry on with the experiment
e: Mercury is poisonous: never touch it.
Mercury must not go down the drain.
Spills must be reported straight away.
pick.y: Report accidents immediately; some substances are dangerous.

pick.q: Which is a safe practice in the laboratory?
w: Tasting a solution to identify it
Running between benches
Hanging a heavy load on a small spring balance
e: Never taste chemicals.
Running causes accidents.
Overloading damages the spring and the load may fall.
pick.y: Goggles protect your eyes from splashes.

pick.q: Why must you not overload a spring balance?
pick.r: The spring can be stretched past its limit and be damaged
w: It makes the reading in kilograms
It changes the value of g
It makes the spring lighter
e: A spring balance reads newtons.
g depends on the planet, not on the balance.
Mass of the spring does not change.
pick.y: Beyond its elastic limit a spring does not return to its shape.

questions.prompt: Find the weight of a {m} kg bag of rice on Earth (g = {10} N/kg).

misconceptions.explain: {m} kg is the mass. Weight is a force: multiply by g = {10} N/kg.
Multiply by g, do not divide.

pick.q: Which statement about mass is true?
pick.r: It is the same on the Earth and on the Moon
w: It is measured in newtons
It is smaller on the Moon
It is measured with a newton meter
e: Mass is measured in kilograms.
The amount of matter does not change.
A newton meter measures force (weight).
pick.y: Mass is the amount of matter: it does not depend on place.

pick.q: Which statement about weight is true?
pick.r: It is a force measured in newtons
w: It is measured in kilograms
It is the same everywhere
It is a scalar
e: Kilograms measure mass.
Weight depends on g, which changes from place to place.
Weight has a direction (down): it is a vector.
pick.y: Weight is the pull of gravity, a force.

pick.q: An astronaut goes to the Moon. What happens?
pick.r: Her weight decreases but her mass stays the same
w: Her mass decreases but her weight stays the same
Both decrease
Both stay the same
e: Mass does not change with place.
Mass does not change with place.
Weight changes because g is smaller on the Moon.
pick.y: g is smaller on the Moon, so W = mg is smaller; m is unchanged.

questions.prompt: A tin of tomato paste has a mass of {m} g. Find its weight on Earth (N).

misconceptions.explain: Change grams to kilograms first: divide by {1000}.
That is the mass in kg. Multiply by g = {10} N/kg.

solution: Change the mass to kilograms: {m} g = {m / 1000} kg.

questions.prompt: A rock has a mass of {m} kg. What is its weight on the Moon, where g = {1.6} N/kg?

misconceptions.explain: That is its weight on Earth. On the Moon g = {1.6} N/kg.
Multiply the mass by g, do not divide.
